headline: 16 governors led by Wes Moore urge Congress to pass SAFE Banking now
dek: Sixteen Democratic governors asked Congress on 9 November to pass the SAFE Banking Act this session, saying rescheduling has not fixed cannabis banking.
key_points: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, led a 9 November letter from 16 Democratic governors urging Congress to pass the SAFE Banking Act.
The governors want action in the current lame-duck session; if the bill is not enacted by the end of the year, it must be reintroduced in the new Congress.
They argue rescheduling leaves banks bound by the same Bank Secrecy Act duties, so cannabis firms still run largely on cash.
Neither chamber has given the 2026 bill (S. 4942 / H.R. 9471) a committee hearing; the House has passed earlier versions seven times, the Senate never.
body: Sixteen governors have asked Congress to pass the SAFE Banking Act before the current session ends, arguing that federal rescheduling has not solved the cash problem facing state-licensed cannabis businesses. The letter, sent to House and Senate leaders on Monday 9 November and led by Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, says the bill would let licensed operators move their money into regulated banks, which the signers frame as a matter of public safety, tax collection and oversight, Marijuana Moment and Cannabis Business Times reported.

All 16 signers are Democrats. Moore, who chairs the National Governors Association, was joined by the governors of Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin. The request is for the lame-duck session, not the next Congress: Cannabis Business Times reported that the governors want the bill finished now, even though Democrats will control both chambers from January.
## What the governors are asking for

The SAFE Banking Act would stop federal banking regulators from penalising banks, credit unions and other financial institutions solely for serving cannabis businesses that comply with state law, with related protections for lending and deposit insurance. The 2026 version was introduced in June as S. 4942 by Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR), with Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Steve Daines among the original cosponsors, and as H.R. 9471 by Rep. Dave Joyce (R-OH), according to The Marijuana Herald.

The governors' case rests on three points. First, cash: operators that cannot get loans, payroll services or card processing hold large sums on site, and the letter says that makes stores, staff and customers targets for robbery. Second, state administration: the signers describe trouble depositing cannabis tax payments and processing licence fees because the proceeds remain federally illegal. Third, enforcement: they argue that bringing the industry into the banking system would give state regulators the Bank Secrecy Act reports that banks file with the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, and with them a clearer view of where cannabis money goes.
The letter also says the bill respects each state's choice to legalise or prohibit cannabis and would not change cannabis's federal classification, according to Cannabis Business Times.
> Rescheduling changed how the DEA sees medical cannabis. It did not change how a compliance officer at a bank sees a dispensary's deposits.
## Why rescheduling did not fix banking

Attorney General Todd Blanche's order of 23 April 2026 moved state-licensed medical cannabis to Schedule III, and a separate proceeding on adult-use cannabis is still under way, as we reported on 7 November when the final briefs in that hearing closed. The governors cite rescheduling as a reason to act, not as a substitute for the bill. Banks that serve the industry still carry Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money-laundering duties, and a Schedule III substance remains a controlled substance.

The Government Accountability Office set out the practical gap in a report publicly released on 8 September (GAO-26-107498). Using FinCEN data, it found that the number of banks and credit unions reporting cannabis-related activity rose from 2015 to 2019 and then held roughly steady through 2024, with about 1,000 institutions filing cannabis-related suspicious activity reports in 2024. Business owners told GAO about account closures, high fees and high loan rates, and said card payments are hard largely because two major card companies prohibit cannabis purchases. Institutions that stay away cited regulatory risk and the cost of compliance.

The bill's record shows how hard the last step is. The House passed versions of SAFE Banking seven times between 2019 and 2022, and the Senate Banking Committee approved a cannabis banking measure in 2023, but no version has ever reached a Senate floor vote. Cannabis Business Times reported that neither chamber has held a committee hearing on the 2026 bill under House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

Some in the industry are careful not to read too much into the midterms. Anthony Coniglio, chief executive of the cannabis property lender NewLake Capital Partners, told Business of Cannabis that a change in leadership does not by itself change that record, though he expects committee gavels to pass to members who have backed reform. Business of Cannabis noted that Sherrod Brown, who chaired Senate Banking under the last Democratic majority and was the bill's leading champion, returns to the Senate in January.
Timing adds pressure. The current Congress ends with the year, and a bill not enacted by then must be reintroduced and start the committee process again in 2027, as The Marijuana Herald noted.
## Who signed, and what it says about the states

The signers are not a list of mature adult-use markets. Using MetaFlora's state legal hubs, at least two signers lead states with no adult-use market at all: Wisconsin, where only CBD products are legal for medical use, and Kentucky, which has a comprehensive medical programme but no adult-use law. Virginia allows adult possession but has no legal retail sales yet. Their governors are asking for a fix to a problem their own markets have barely begun to face, which suggests the case is being made as a state-finance and policing argument rather than an industry one.

The letter is also a partisan document for a bill with bipartisan sponsors. No Republican governor signed, even though the Senate bill's original cosponsors include two Republicans and the House sponsor is a Republican. Five of the signers, in Colorado, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico and Wisconsin, leave office in January, Cannabis Business Times reported. A bipartisan group of 32 state and territorial attorneys general sent a similar request in 2025, and the American Bankers Association urged Congress in July to pass cannabis banking legislation.

Watch whether Senate or House leaders schedule any committee action before the session ends; without a hearing, passage this year would need the bill to ride on must-pass legislation. The same weeks run up to 11 December, when the federal hemp THC limit is due to start. From January, watch who takes the Senate Banking gavel and whether the bill is reintroduced in the opening weeks of the new Congress. Separately, the DEA's adult-use rescheduling decision remains pending; it would widen the tax relief but, on the governors' own account, would not settle the banking question.
